Measuring Morphological Productivity: Building Computational Tools for Historical English Analysis
April 30, 2026
Describes the development process of a model for automated morphological segmentation and demonstrates the model’s application to the Corpus of Late Modern English Texts (CLMET). Beginning with Wiktionary’s morphological data (~300,000 words), we developed systematic auditing to ensure models learn historically accurate patterns. Three challenges emerged: (1) consistency—standardizing contributor conventions (-d vs. -ed); (2) etymological fidelity—balancing synchronic and diachronic analysis (e.g., treating wriggle as monomorphemic in training data while preserving the historical wrig_le boundary in metadata for diachronic research); (3) temporal sensitivity—avoiding anachronistic decomposition of loans like naïveté.

February 19, 2026

Here are some of the main takeaways:

Although ChatGPT seemed to explode into the public consciousness, it is part of a surprisingly long history of technological development.
Understanding at least some of that history can help us understand the affordances and limitations of LLMs. They kind of seem like magic, but they’re not.
ChatGPT and other LLMs are also part of the inextricable relationship between writing and technology, which doesn’t mean that they don’t present their own unique problems and challenges.
Research is showing that the writing produced by LLMs don’t much look like human writing in a number of important ways, which doesn’t mean that students shouldn’t use them. However, they should be aware that they may not always be performing in the way that they think.

text:
February 19, 2026
    View slides in full screen
       
      
    
  


This presentation addresses a critical pedagogical challenge: writing instructors increasingly report an intuitive “feeling” that something is wrong with LLM-generated academic writing, yet lack concrete language to discuss these differences with students. We introduce multivariate sentiment analysis as both a research methodology and an accessible teaching tool for making visible the affective dimensions that distinguish human academic writing from LLM outputs.



The Pedagogical Problem: Instructors recognize inappropriate tone and excessive positivity in LLM writing but lack systematic methods to identify and discuss these differences with students and instructors.
Our Approach: Using the GoEmotions sentiment analysis model (28 emotion categories) applied to the Human-AI Parallel Corpus v2 in English (HAP-E-2), we quantify what experienced writers intuitively recognize, transforming impressionistic observations into teachable knowledge.
Key Findings:

GPT-4o uses approximately 4x more approval language than human academic writers (31.7% vs. 8.3%) and expresses that approval with broader scope and less hedging
Human academic writing maintains 88.6% neutral language compared to GPT-4o’s 65.5%
Different LLM models exhibit distinct emotional patterns that vary from human writing in different ways—highlighting that these register differences will persist as models evolve

Pedagogical Implications: Sentiment analysis provides accessible metalanguage (approval, admiration, disapproval) for discussing register appropriateness, enabling instructors to transform vague warnings (“this doesn’t sound right”) into evidence-based explanations and helping students develop critical awareness of when emotional register deviates from disciplinary norms.
The Power of Naming: By providing concrete, measurable patterns, we transform instructor helplessness into informed teaching and give students agency to make deliberate choices about when and how to use generative AI tools in ways that enhance rather than limit their academic development.





Our recent PNAS study: Do LLMs Write like Humans — examining broader implications of LLMs for knowledge production
Our earlier studies of student writing: Written Communication — examining how student academic writing differs from expert and AI-generated texts; Journal of Statistics and Data Science Education — comparing patterns in statistical reports authored by LLMs to those authored by students and by published researchers
International application: Stylistic Benchmark for Czech — researchers applying our methodological approach to Czech language texts, demonstrating the cross-linguistic potential of sentiment analysis for understanding LLM-generated writing
HAP-E-2 Corpus: Available at Hugging Face for researchers interested in comparative LLM analysis

Excerpts from texts produced by ChatGPT

On the other, their content can range from vague, to ambiguous, to vapid. (What exactly is “a comprehensive dataset encompassing [..] healthcare utilization”?) At issue here is what pertinent information is compressed out of these phrases.

title: How Did We Get to LLMs?
text:
Implications
Key takeaways

ChatGPT produces sentences that are more informationally dense than that of student writing, but the information density is created using repetitive grammatical patterns.
Machine-generated writing demonstrates less modulation of stress or confidence.
Broadly, LLMs are not as grammatically nimble as human writers.
LLM-generated text generally produces academic prose expressing limited engagement with core, disciplinary concepts either in the way that experts do or in the way that novice students do. (Though LLMs can arrive at something more like expert writing with iterative prompting.)
It is a open question as to the effects of LLMs on the development of students’ disciplinary expertise.

title: Large Language Models
text:
Implications
Key takeaways


ChatGPT produces sentences that are more informationally dense than that of human writing, but the information density is expressed using repetitive grammatical patterns.
The tendency toward greater information density appears to be magnified by reinforcement learning (also called instruction tuning), though the reasons for that magnification are unclear.
Machine-generated writing demonstrates less modulation of stress or confidence.
Broadly, LLMs are not as grammatically nimble as human writers.
LLM-generated text generally produces academic prose expressing limited engagement with core, disciplinary concepts either in the way that experts do or in the way that novice students do. (Though LLMs can arrive at something more like expert writing with iterative prompting.)

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI
text:
The Pedagogical Problem
“Something feels wrong about this writing…”

Writing instructors increasingly report an intuitive “feeling” that something is wrong with LLM-generated academic writing:

Inappropriate tone
Excessive positivity

What researchers call “sycophancy” (e.g., Singh et al. 2026; Perez et al. 2022)



But this intuition leaves us helpless:

No concrete language to discuss with students
No systematic methods to identify differences
Vague warnings: “This doesn’t sound right” or “ChatGPT doesn’t write like a scholar”

Using multivariate sentiment to make visible what experienced writers intuitively recognize

Advantages over traditional approaches

Dictionary-based stance/engagement studies:

Excellent for specific lexical patterns (e.g., hedges, boosters)

Limited to predetermined word lists

Multivariate sentiment analysis:

Captures broader affective range (28 emotion categories)
Uses contextual understanding (not just word lists)
More intuitive for students: “approval,” “admiration,” “disapproval”
Reveals patterns dictionary searches miss

A much more pronounced gap

Human academic writing:

88.6% neutral language
8.3% approval, 1.0% admiration
Careful, hedged claims

GPT-4o academic writing:

The Quality of Approval Matters
Not just how much, but how it’s expressed

Human academic writer (hedged, scoped):

“International mobility may, in turn, have a positive impact on large distance collaborations as mobile inventors act as bridges across teams…”

GPT-4o (emphatic, broad scope):

“The marriage of these approaches fosters a more nuanced appreciation of the Earth’s complex systems, empowering us to address the pressing environmental and engineering challenges of our time.”



Both tagged as “approval” — but the register appropriateness differs dramatically

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI
text:
Sycophancy Quantified
What instructors intuitively recognize

GPT-4o doesn’t just use more positive language — it expresses emphatic approval in contexts where human academic writers employ:

Hedges (may, might, could)
Carefully scoped claims (specific, limited contexts)
Neutral or slightly positive evaluations

This mirrors common novice writing problems:

Claims that are too broad
Excessive enthusiasm without supporting evidence
Inappropriate emotional intensity for academic contexts

From Intuition to Instruction
The power of naming

Instead of: “This doesn’t sound right”
We can say: “GPT-4o uses 4x more approval language than human academic writers and expresses that approval with broader scope and less hedging”
This specificity helps students:

Understand what makes LLM output inappropriate
Develop critical awareness of register and tone
Make informed decisions about when/how to use LLMs

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI
text:
Developing Critical AI Literacy
Transferable skills, not model-specific fixes

Students learn to recognize:

When approval or admiration in their drafts exceeds disciplinary norms
How emotional register signals expertise vs. novice writing
Why different rhetorical situations require different affective stances

Not memorizing: “GPT-4o uses too much approval language”
But developing: General awareness of emotional appropriateness in academic writing

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI
text:
Classroom Applications
From research to practice

Writing analytics assignments:

Students analyze LLM outputs using sentiment analysis frameworks
Compare emotional patterns in expert vs. novice vs. AI writing
Develop metacognitive awareness about genre and register

Revision practices:

Add emotional register to revision checklists
Ask: “Does this approval seem appropriately scoped?”
Consider: “Is my claim hedged at the right level?”

Contrastive rhetoric:

Have students identify inappropriate emotional patterns in LLM outputs
Build critical awareness by probing tools for limitations

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI

Equity and Access
Supporting students and instructors

Why sentiment analysis particularly helps:

Makes tacit conventions explicit
Provides accessible metalanguage (no linguistics degree needed)
Scaffolds understanding of disciplinary emotional norms

Result: More equitable access to academic discourse conventions

Why Emotions Matter in Academic Writing
An accessible entry point

Sentiment analysis provides:

Intuitive categories students can understand
Concrete data instructors can reference
Bridge between computational analysis and rhetorical awareness

Complements traditional approaches:

Lexical bundles → specific phrases to use
Sentiment analysis → broader register appropriateness

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI
text:
Methodological Trade-offs
What we gain and what we sacrifice

What sentiment analysis doesn’t do:

Provide specific lexical bundles (“use may instead of will”)
Identify exact stance markers to teach
Replace dictionary-based corpus linguistics

What sentiment analysis does do:

Capture broader emotional impressions across many features
Work with contextual understanding (not just word lists)
Provide accessible framework for non-linguists
Scale to large corpora efficiently
Quantify what experienced writers recognize intuitively

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI
text:
Key Takeaways


LLMs produce measurably different emotional registers — especially in academic writing
Patterns vary across models and will continue to shift with updates
Need stable frameworks, not model-specific knowledge
Sentiment analysis provides accessible metalanguage for discussing register appropriateness
Equity matters: Explicit instruction benefits those who struggle most with tacit conventions

title: Beyond the “Feeling” of AI
text:
Conclusion
The Power of Naming

By quantifying the affective dimensions of academic writing, we transform:

Instructor helplessness → informed, strategic teaching
Vague intuitions → concrete, shareable knowledge

Impressionistic warnings → evidence-based explanations

We give students agency:

To recognize inappropriate emotional register
To evaluate LLM outputs critically
To make deliberate choices about when and how to use these tools

In ways that enhance — not limit — their academic development

Excerpts of ChatGPT-generated writing with Noun + Noun and Adj. + Noun sequences underlined in blue and other characteristic features of machine-generated writing marked in red.




The LLM has a propensity to condense information into chunked noun phrases, constructed as either noun + noun or adjective + noun sequences. Such sequences are sometimes aggregated using the coordinator and. On the one hand, these phrases can project a kind of authoritative voice. On the other, their content can range from vague, to ambiguous, to vapid. (What exactly is “a comprehensive dataset encompassing [..] healthcare utilization”?)

title: Large Language Models 🎃
text:
Implications
Key takeaways


ChatGPT produces sentences that are more informationally dense than that of human writing, but the information density is expressed using repetitive grammatical patterns.
The tendency toward greater information density appears to be magnified by reinforcement learning (also called instruction tuning), though the reasons for that magnification are unclear.
Machine-generated writing demonstrates less modulation of stress or confidence.
Broadly, LLMs are not as grammatically nimble as human writers.
LLM-generated text generally produces academic prose expressing limited engagement with core, disciplinary concepts either in the way that experts do or in the way that novice students do. (Though LLMs can arrive at something more like expert writing with iterative prompting.)

title: Measuring Morphological Productivity
text:
Overview
Problem

How to measure morphological productivity and changes in morphological productivity over time?
Traditional use of hapax legomenon as a proxy has known limitiations (sensitive to corpus size, most data is discarded, etc.) (Pankratz et al. 2022, 2025; Feltgen 2025; Baayen 2008).
Automatic segmentation is challenging (Baayen et al. 2011).

title: Measuring Morphological Productivity
text:
Overview
Solution

Train a model that can reliably segment large corpora accurately and effeciently.
Create a Python package to orchestrate processing and segmentation.
Use segmentation as an analytic bridge between raw token data and productivity measures.

text:
Development
Example of the lexicalization problem — historical affixes that are not typically segmentable in Present Day English:

Frequentive: giggle, wriggle, dazzle, twinkle
Instrumental: handle, ladle
Adjectival (prone to): brittle

title: Measuring Morphological Productivity
text:
Development
Model and model training


Base model: ByT5-small, fine-tuned for English morphological segmentation.
Task formulation: word in, segmented morpheme string out.
Why byte-level modeling:

avoids dependence on a fixed subword vocabulary
handles orthographic variation, apostrophes, doubled letters, and low-frequency forms more naturally
remains open-vocabulary, which matters for historical and uncommon lexical items

Why seq2seq generation rather than token classification: generating the segmented string directly is more natural than predicting a label for each character and reconstructing the output afterward.
Main tradeoff: byte-level modeling is slower than subword approaches, so caching and batching support in the package matters.


Results: Loss: 0.0404 — Exact Match: 0.9474

title: Measuring Morphological Productivity
text:
Development
Package architecture


The package is organized in layers, from low-level inference to high-level analysis.
At the base: a parser that segments words, and a cache that stores results so large corpora don’t have to be re-parsed from scratch.
Above that: a decomposition layer that can break complex morpheme strings into their constituent parts. The depth of decomposition is adjustable — useful because different research questions call for different levels of morphological detail.
At the top: a productivity layer that turns segmented tokens into analysis-ready tables, and a higher-level analyzer that handles the full workflow end-to-end.
The analyzer also integrates with spaCy: token processing can draw on spaCy’s POS tags and morphological attributes, and the model’s segmentation output can be checked against spaCy’s own morph analysis. This provides a practical validation layer and allows the two sources of morphological information to complement each other.
The package also ships with curated internal resources — affix metadata, decomposition maps, a protected monomorpheme list — so it works out of the box without external configuration.

title: Measuring Morphological Productivity
text:
Development
Key choices and affordances


The package is built around token-frequency input rather than around one corpus-processing stack.
The core install is analysis-focused, while prep and audit workflows are optional.
Caching is treated as part of the design, not as an afterthought.
Multiple decomposition strategies are exposed because different research questions want different levels of morphological depth.
Role labels are inferred from supporting evidence rather than treated as fixed truths.
The main affordances are:

quick single-word inspection
batch parsing for corpus inventories
reusable cached parsing
productivity summaries over time
support tables that move from abstract measures back to example words and bases
a higher-level analyzer workflow for researchers who do not want to wire the entire pipeline by hand

title: Measuring Morphological Productivity
text:
Development
Current development status

The project now includes a reusable package, not just a trained model.
Core modules are in place for parsing, caching, decomposition, analyzer workflows, productivity summaries, affix metadata, and matrix transforms.
Optional prep modules exist for auditing training data and rebuilding package resources.
Versioned resources are already bundled with the library.
The codebase has broad automated test coverage across parser behavior, productivity logic, decomposition, caching, affix resources, and corpus preprocessing.
The package is still pre-release, but it is already usable as a research workflow.

title: Measuring Morphological Productivity
text:
Example
Table values


N: total token count contributed by this morpheme in the preview sample.
V: number of distinct word types containing the morpheme in this final-segment slice.
V1: number of hapax types, i.e. types that occur once in the sample.
F, Y, I: diversity and productivity summaries. Read them comparatively across rows rather than as standalone verdicts.
P baayen: hapax-based productivity, useful for asking whether a suffix appears to be recruiting new types in the sample.
S baayen: expansion potential relative to the observed vocabulary in the sample.
H and H norm: entropy-based dispersion measures that help distinguish concentrated rows from rows spread across many types.
dominant morpheme family, dominant morpheme function, and dominant role confidence: the current best role label inferred from the supporting token evidence.

Here are some of the main takeaways:

Although ChatGPT seemed to explode into the public consciousness, it is part of a surprisingly long history of technological development.
Understanding at least some of that history can help us understand the affordances and limitations of LLMs. They kind of seem like magic, but they’re not.
ChatGPT and other LLMs are also part of the inextricable relationship between writing and technology, which doesn’t mean that they don’t present their own unique problems and challenges.
Research is showing that the writing produced by LLMs don’t much look like human writing in a number of important ways, which doesn’t mean that writers (whether students, instructors, or professionals) shouldn’t use them. However, they should be aware that they may not always be performing in the way that they think.
